text: A trade secret is confidential business information that provides competitive advantage. Unlike patents (which require disclosure), trade secrets protect by maintaining secrecy. Types: formulas, recipes, processes, customer lists, business strategies, know-how. Famous examples: Coca-Cola formula, KFC recipe. For AYUSH: traditional family recipes, proprietary extraction processes, supplier relationships, pricing strategies. No registration required — protection through confidentiality. Advantages: no disclosure, no time limit, no fees. Disadvantages: no protection once secret is out, difficult to enforce.

India has no specific trade secret statute. Protection through: 1) Contract law — breach of confidentiality agreements. 2) Common law — breach of confidence doctrine. 3) Equity — courts protect confidential information. 4) IPC Section 405/408 — criminal breach of trust (limited). Key case: American Express Bank Ltd v Priya Puri — court recognized trade secrets as property, granted injunction. For AYUSH: rely on strong contracts (NDAs, employment agreements) and document confidentiality measures.

For information to qualify as trade secret: 1) SECRECY — not generally known or readily ascertainable. 2) COMMERCIAL VALUE — derives value from being secret. 3) REASONABLE EFFORTS — owner takes measures to maintain secrecy. If any element missing, no trade secret protection. For AYUSH formulations: document that formula is kept secret, limit access to need-to-know personnel, use NDAs, don't publish full details. If you patent it (full disclosure), it's no longer a trade secret.

When to choose trade secret over patent: 1) Information can be kept secret indefinitely (not reverse-engineerable). 2) Patent protection unavailable (methods of treatment, traditional knowledge). 3) Want protection beyond 20 years. 4) Don't want to disclose to competitors. When to choose patent: 1) Product can be reverse-engineered. 2) Need to stop competitors with injunction. 3) Want to license the technology. 4) Want to attract investors (IP portfolio value). For AYUSH: if formulation is in final product and can be analyzed, patent is better; if process know-how is key, trade secret may work.

Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) are essential for trade secret protection. Key clauses: 1) Definition of confidential information (specific, comprehensive). 2) Obligations of receiving party (maintain secrecy, limit use, limit access). 3) Exclusions (publicly known, independently developed, legally obtained). 4) Duration (reasonable period, can be indefinite for true secrets). 5) Return/destruction of information on termination. 6) Remedies for breach (injunction, damages, indemnity). For AYUSH: use NDAs with employees, suppliers, manufacturers, potential partners, investors. One-way or mutual depending on relationship.

Employees are the biggest trade secret risk. Protections: 1) Employment agreement with confidentiality clause. 2) Separate NDA if particularly sensitive role. 3) Training on confidentiality obligations. 4) Access controls — need-to-know basis. 5) Exit interviews reminding of obligations. 6) Post-employment restrictions (non-compete limited enforceability in India, but confidentiality survives). 7) Monitor for suspicious activity before departure. For AYUSH R&D teams: formulation scientists should have strong confidentiality terms; consider trade secret bonuses tied to compliance.

Trade secret protection requires security measures: Physical: 1) Locked files/safes for documents. 2) Restricted area access (key cards, biometrics). 3) Visitor logs and escort policies. 4) Clean desk policy. 5) Document labeling ('Confidential'). Digital: 1) Password protection, encryption. 2) Access controls (role-based). 3) Audit trails. 4) Secure networks, VPNs. 5) Data loss prevention software. 6) Secure disposal (shredding, wiping). For AYUSH manufacturing: physical security of formulation rooms, restricted access to batch records, secure storage of master formulas.

If trade secret is misappropriated, remedies available: 1) Injunction — stop use/disclosure (most important). 2) Damages — compensate for losses. 3) Account of profits — if defendant profited. 4) Delivery up — return/destroy misappropriated information. Challenges in India: proving breach, valuing damages, speed of court process. Courts have granted injunctions in trade secret cases (John Richard Brady v Chemical Process Equipments). For AYUSH: if competitor hires your R&D head and suddenly launches similar product, act fast with injunction application.

Reverse engineering — analyzing a product to discover its composition/design — is generally legal if the product was legitimately obtained. If someone buys your AYUSH product and analyzes it to discover the formulation, that's not trade secret misappropriation. Implication: if your secret can be discovered by analyzing the commercial product, trade secret protection is weak. For AYUSH: complex processes, specific parameters, know-how in manufacturing are harder to reverse-engineer than simple ingredient lists. Consider what's truly protectable.

Know-how (practical knowledge, skills, techniques) is often licensed even without patent. Know-how license agreements include: 1) Definition of know-how being licensed. 2) Scope of license (exclusive/non-exclusive, territory, field). 3) Technical assistance and training. 4) Confidentiality obligations. 5) Improvements clause — who owns improvements. 6) Royalty/fee structure. 7) Term and termination. For AYUSH: license manufacturing know-how to partners without disclosing full formula — provide training on-site, maintain some control.

In mergers and acquisitions, trade secrets are valuable assets. Due diligence includes: 1) Identifying trade secrets. 2) Verifying confidentiality measures in place. 3) Checking for prior breaches or disputes. 4) Assessing risk of key employee departure. 5) Valuing the trade secrets. Sellers should: inventory trade secrets, document protection measures, ensure clean chain of custody. Buyers should: conduct thorough DD, get representations and warranties, plan for integration and continued protection. For AYUSH acquisition: formulation know-how often the main asset — protect through deal structure.

Sharing trade secrets with partners (manufacturers, distributors, JV partners) requires careful management: 1) Disclose only what's necessary for the relationship. 2) Strong NDA before any disclosure. 3) Tiered disclosure — more as trust builds. 4) Control access — don't give full picture to any one partner. 5) Audit rights to verify compliance. 6) Exit provisions — what happens to information on termination. For AYUSH contract manufacturers: they need enough to make the product, but consider keeping some aspects (final blending, specific ratios) in-house.
